analysis.one_liner: Cuts the tax rate on investment gains in half and triples the losses investors can deduct.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut the tax rate on capital gains — the profit from selling stocks, real estate, or other assets held more than a year — roughly in half, taking the top rate from 20% to 10% and eliminating the lowest rate entirely. It would also have tripled, from $3,000 to $10,000, the amount of investment losses an individual can subtract from wages and other income each year when figuring taxes, with the cap rising with inflation. Both changes were framed as economic stimulus. The bill was sent to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that own stocks, real estate, and other appreciated assets would pay less tax when they sell. Because most capital gains income goes to the highest-earning households, the rate cut would flow mostly to the wealthy. The larger loss deduction would also help small and mid-level investors who sold at a loss, including people who sold a home or a small amount of stock. The bill's sponsors framed both changes as economic stimulus.

how_it_helps.text: It would cut the tax rate on long-term capital gains: the lowest rate would go from 10% to 0%, and the top rate from 20% to 10%, starting in 2003.
It would raise the amount of capital losses an individual can deduct against ordinary income each year from $3,000 to $10,000, and index that amount to inflation.
The changes would apply to tax years beginning after December 31, 2002, so they would take effect immediately upon enactment.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would collect less revenue, which means other taxpayers or future taxpayers bear the cost through larger deficits unless spending is cut. Ordinary taxpayers with little or no investment income would get essentially nothing from the rate cut and would effectively help finance the reduction for wealthier investors.

drawbacks.text: Cutting the capital gains rate would reduce federal revenue, and because capital gains income is concentrated among the wealthiest households, most of the lost revenue would be a tax cut for the top of the income distribution.

The bill's only provision aimed at ordinary taxpayers, raising the capital loss deduction, is capped at $10,000, so it does little for anyone with significant investments while the rate cut mainly benefits large holders.

Allowing more capital losses to offset ordinary income would let investors deduct more of their investment losses against wages and salary, adding complexity to tax filings and offering a partial tax shelter for losses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The loss-deduction increase was a real but modest help to small investors, and its cost to the Treasury was small. The rate cut was the bill's centerpiece, and because the overwhelming share of capital gains goes to households in the top income brackets, its revenue cost would have flowed overwhelmingly to the top of the income distribution. As deficit-financed stimulus, the rate cut offered the least benefit per dollar of revenue lost. An honest supporter could defend the loss-deduction change easily and the rate cut only with difficulty.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never came out, so it never got a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 29, 2003 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever recorded, through the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005.

The bill would have cut the top capital gains rate from 20% to 10% and the bottom rate from 10% to 0%, and raised the annual capital loss deduction from $3,000 to $10,000, effective for tax years after 2002.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, capital gains taxes stayed at their existing rates, so the federal Treasury kept revenue it would have lost. Investors who would have paid lower taxes gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal Treasury kept the revenue

for.name: Rep. J. D. Hayworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill cutting capital gains rates and raising the loss deduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill never advanced far enough for a roll call that would show whether any Democrats supported it.

industries.industry: Investors with appreciated assets (individuals and estates)
industries.note: The bill would cut their tax rate on gains by half or more and triple the losses they can deduct against other income. Most capital gains go to the wealthiest households, so most of the benefit lands there.

Lower taxes on selling assets encourages more trading and makes investment products more attractive, benefiting brokers, mutual funds, and asset managers. No direct cost to the industry; the cost falls on the federal Treasury.
Listed as the paying side: the bill would cut federal revenue with no offset, so other taxpayers or federal borrowing would absorb the cost.
